title: Orthogonality in Inner Product Spaces (6.2)
description: Day 36: orthogonality depends on the inner product, Cauchy–Schwarz, angles, triangle inequality, Generalized Pythagoras, and orthogonal complements in weighted, matrix, polynomial, and function spaces. 10 questions pulled per attempt from a pool of 60.

questions.prompt: Vectors $u$ and $v$ in an inner product space are called orthogonal when $\langle u,v\rangle=$ _____.
questions.explanation: Orthogonal means the inner product is zero.

questions.prompt: Whether two vectors are orthogonal depends on which inner product is being used.
explanations: For example $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are orthogonal for the dot product but not for $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$.

questions.prompt: If $u\perp v$ for the dot product on $\mathbb R^2$, then $u\perp v$ for every inner product on $\mathbb R^2$.
explanations: Counterexample: $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ under the weighted product $3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$ give $3-2=1\ne0$.

questions.prompt: The zero vector is orthogonal to every vector in an inner product space.
A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality says $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le$ _____.
questions.explanation: The inner product is at most the product of the lengths in absolute value.

questions.prompt: Cauchy–Schwarz holds in every real inner product space, not just $\mathbb R^n$ with the dot product.
explanations: It is proved from the four axioms alone, so it holds for functions, matrices, polynomials, and every other inner product.

questions.prompt: Equality $|\langle u,v\rangle|=\|u\|\|v\|$ holds exactly when:
explanations: $u=v$ gives equality, but so does $u=-3v$. Dependence is the full condition.
Unit length does not force equality. Two orthogonal unit vectors give $0<1$.
Orthogonal vectors give $|\langle u,v\rangle|=0$, which is the far-from-equality case.

questions.prompt: In an inner product space, the angle $\theta$ between nonzero $u$ and $v$ is defined by $\cos\theta=$ _____.
questions.explanation: Same formula as in $\mathbb R^n$, with the general inner product.

questions.prompt: Why is the angle formula legitimate in a general inner product space?
choices: Because the triangle inequality says so
Because every inner product space is secretly $\mathbb R^n$
Cauchy–Schwarz guarantees the fraction lies in $[-1,1]$, so $\arccos$ is defined
explanations: The triangle inequality is a consequence of Cauchy–Schwarz, not the reason the angle exists.
Function and matrix spaces are not $\mathbb R^n$ with the dot product.
Norms can be any nonnegative number.

questions.prompt: If $\langle u,v\rangle<0$ for nonzero $u,v$, the angle between them is greater than $90^\circ$.
If the angle between nonzero $u$ and $v$ is $0^\circ$, then $u$ is a positive scalar multiple of $v$.
explanations: $\cos\theta=1$ is equality in Cauchy–Schwarz with $\langle u,v\rangle>0$.

questions.prompt: The triangle inequality says $\|u+v\|\le$ _____.
questions.explanation: The direct path is never longer than the detour.

questions.prompt: Generalized Pythagorean Theorem: if $u\perp v$, then $\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2$.
explanations: $\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2$ and the middle term is $0$.

questions.prompt: In a real inner product space, if $\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2$, then $u\perp v$.
For orthogonal $u,v$ we have $\|u+v\|=\|u\|+\|v\|$.
explanations: Orthogonal vectors give $\|u+v\|=\sqrt{\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2}$, which is smaller. Equality in the triangle inequality needs the same direction.

questions.prompt: If $\|u\|=2$, $\|v\|=3$ and $\langle u,v\rangle=1$, find $\|u+v\|^2$.
If $\|u\|=2$, $\|v\|=3$ and $\langle u,v\rangle=1$, find $\|u-v\|^2$.
Given $\|u\|=5$ and $\|v\|=2$, which value of $\langle u,v\rangle$ is impossible?
Given $\|u\|=3$ and $\|v\|=4$, which value is NOT possible for $\|u+v\|$?
explanations: Possible when $u$ and $v$ point in the same direction.
Possible when $u$ and $v$ point in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: $W^\perp=\{v:\langle v,w\rangle=$ _____ for every $w$ in $W\}$.
questions.explanation: The orthogonal complement is everything orthogonal to all of $W$.

questions.prompt: For any subspace $W$ of an inner product space $V$, $W^\perp$ is a subspace of $V$.
explanations: Bilinearity: sums and scalar multiples of vectors orthogonal to $W$ are still orthogonal to $W$.

questions.prompt: $W\cap W^\perp=\{0\}$.
explanations: If $w$ is in both, $\langle w,w\rangle=0$, so $w=0$ by positivity.

questions.prompt: If $V$ is finite-dimensional and $W$ is a subspace, then $\dim W+\dim W^\perp=\dim V$.
explanations: The two pieces fill out the whole space.

questions.prompt: If $\dim V=7$ and $\dim W=3$, find $\dim W^\perp$.
Let $W=\text{span}\{w_1,w_2,w_3\}$. To show $v\in W^\perp$ it is enough to check that:
explanations: That is a condition on the $w$'s, not on $v$.
Length has nothing to do with it.

questions.prompt: If $V$ is finite-dimensional then $(W^\perp)^\perp=W$.
explanations: The complement of the complement returns to the original subspace.

questions.prompt: The orthogonal complement of a subspace $W$ depends on which inner product is used on $V$.
explanations: For $W=\text{span}\{(1,2,3)\}$ the dot product and $\langle u,v\rangle=u_1v_1+2u_2v_2+3u_3v_3$ give different planes.

questions.prompt: In $\mathbb R^2$ with the dot product, which vector spans $W^\perp$ for $W=\text{span}\{(3,4)\}$?
explanations: Its dot product with $(3,4)$ is $7$, not $0$.

questions.prompt: In $\mathbb R^3$ with the dot product, find $\dim W^\perp$ for $W=\text{span}\{(1,2,3)\}$.
Under $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$, which vector spans $\text{span}\{(2,1)\}^\perp$?
explanations: That is the dot-product answer. Here $\langle(2,1),(-1,2)\rangle=-6+4=-2$.

questions.prompt: Under $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$, find $k$ so that $(1,k)\perp(2,3)$.
In $P_2$ with $\langle p,q\rangle=\int_{-1}^{1}pq\,dx$, which polynomial is in $\text{span}\{1\}^\perp$?
On $M_{22}$ with $\langle U,V\rangle=\text{tr}(U^TV)$, which matrix is orthogonal to $I_2$?
With $\langle U,V\rangle=\text{tr}(U^TV)$ on $M_{22}$, every symmetric matrix is orthogonal to every skew-symmetric matrix.
On $M_{22}$ with $\langle U,V\rangle=\text{tr}(U^TV)$, find $\dim W^\perp$ where $W$ is the space of symmetric matrices.
On $M_{22}$ with $\langle U,V\rangle=\text{tr}(U^TV)$, find the dimension of $\text{span}\{I_2\}^\perp$ (the traceless matrices).
Under $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$, compute $\langle(1,2),(2,-1)\rangle$.
Under $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$, compute $\|(2,-3)\|^2$.
Let $\langle u,v\rangle=u^TMv$ with $M=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&5\end{bmatrix}$. Compute $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle$.
With the same $M$, compute $\|e_2\|^2$.
With the same $M$, what is $\cos\theta$ for the angle between $e_1$ and $e_2$?
explanations: $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle=2\ne0$, so they are not orthogonal here.

questions.prompt: In $C[0,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1fg\,dx$, the angle between $1$ and $x$ is:
explanations: They are not multiples of each other.

questions.prompt: In $C[0,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1fg\,dx$, compute $\langle1,x^2\rangle$. (Enter a fraction like 1/4.)
In $C[0,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1fg\,dx$, compute $\langle x,x^3\rangle$. (Enter a fraction.)
In $C[0,1]$ with $\int_0^1fg\,dx$, what is $\cos\theta$ for $f=x$ and $g=x^3$?
explanations: That is only the numerator $\langle x,x^3\rangle$.

questions.prompt: In $C[-1,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-1}^1fg\,dx$, the functions $x$ and $x^2$ are orthogonal.
In $C[0,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1fg\,dx$, the functions $x$ and $x^2$ are orthogonal.
explanations: $\int_0^1x^3\,dx=1/4\ne0$. The interval is part of the inner product.

questions.prompt: In $C[-\pi,\pi]$ with $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}fg\,dx$, which pair is NOT orthogonal?
In $C[-\pi,\pi]$ with $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}fg\,dx$, compute $\|\sin x\|^2$. (Enter a multiple of pi, like 3pi.)
In $C[-\pi,\pi]$ with $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}fg\,dx$, compute $\|\sin x+\cos x\|^2$. (Use Pythagoras. Enter a multiple of pi.)
On $P_2$ with $\langle p,q\rangle=p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)$, compute $\langle x^2,\,1+x\rangle$.
questions.explanation: $x^2$ takes values $1,0,1$ and $1+x$ takes values $0,1,2$, so the sum is $0+0+2=2$.

questions.prompt: In $C[0,1]$ with $\int_0^1fg\,dx$, find $c$ so that $x^2+c\perp1$. (Enter a fraction.)
In $C[0,2]$ with $\int_0^2fg\,dx$, find $c$ so that $x^2+c\perp1$. (Enter a fraction.)
In $C[0,1]$, $\left(\int_0^1x\,dx\right)^2\le\int_0^1x^2\,dx$.
Under $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$, which is a unit vector orthogonal to $(2,1)$?
explanations: That is the dot-product answer, not orthogonal here.
That normalizes with the Euclidean length. Here $\|(1,-3)\|^2=3+18=21$.

questions.prompt: Using Cauchy–Schwarz with $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$ and $v=(\tfrac13,\tfrac12)$, the smallest $k$ with $(x+y)^2\le k(3x^2+2y^2)$ for all $x,y$ is:
Under $\langle u,v\rangle=3u_1v_1+2u_2v_2$, let $u=(2,1)$ and $v=(1,-3)$. Compute $\|u+v\|^2$.
On $M_{22}$ with $\langle U,V\rangle=\text{tr}(U^TV)$, find $\|K\|^2$ for the skew part $K=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1/2\\1/2&0\end{bmatrix}$ of $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$. (Enter a fraction.)
